excerpt: What to say — and what not to say — when an insurance adjuster calls after a crash in Georgia or South Carolina, and why recorded statements are risky.
keyTakeaways: After a car accident in Georgia or South Carolina, you have no obligation to speak with the at-fault driver's insurer. Never give recorded statements without legal counsel. Georgia uses modified comparative fault under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33 (less than 50%), South Carolina allows recovery at 51% or less. Filing deadlines: 2 years in GA (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33), 3 years in SC (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Avoid admitting fault or saying you feel fine.

faqs.question: Do I have to talk to the other driver's insurance company after an accident?
faqs.answer: No. You have no legal obligation to speak with the at-fault driver's insurance company in Georgia or South Carolina. You can politely decline and refer them to your attorney. You do have a contractual duty to cooperate with your own insurer.

faqs.question: Should I give a recorded statement to an insurance adjuster?
faqs.answer: You should not give a recorded statement to the at-fault driver's insurer without consulting an attorney first. There is no law requiring it, and recorded statements can be selectively quoted to minimize or deny your claim.

faqs.question: What should I say when an insurance adjuster calls after my accident?
faqs.answer: Provide only basic information: your name, contact details, and the date and location of the accident. Do not discuss fault, your injuries in detail, or say you are fine. State that you are still receiving medical treatment and prefer to have your attorney handle further communications.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a car accident claim in Georgia and South Carolina?
faqs.answer: Georgia's statute of limitations is 2 years from the accident date (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). South Carolina allows 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Missing these deadlines typically bars your claim.

faqs.question: What is a lowball settlement offer and should I accept it?
faqs.answer: A lowball offer is an initial settlement amount far below the true value of your claim, often made within days of the accident before you understand your full injuries. You should not accept any settlement without consulting an attorney, as signing a release permanently closes your claim.

faqs.question: Can my social media posts hurt my insurance claim?
faqs.answer: Yes. Insurance companies routinely monitor claimants' social media accounts. Photos of physical activities, check-ins at events, or posts about your daily life can be used to argue your injuries are not as severe as claimed. Limit social media activity during your claim.
